original.title: How Ideas Spread: Whose Norms Matter? Norm Localization and Institutional Change in Asian Regionalism

core_idea: International norms do not simply diffuse from global to local. Local actors actively select, reinterpret and graft external norms onto existing local beliefs and practices, so that the norm fits local identity and legitimacy. Acharya shows this with Southeast Asian regionalism: norms are more likely to take hold when they can be localized.
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: How was an international norm or policy (human rights, gender equality, anti-corruption, education standards) adopted, adapted or resisted in a country or region?
What role do local actors and traditions play in shaping how global norms are used?
Typical data: policy documents, interviews with officials and civil society, process tracing, comparative case studies.
common_mistakes: Treating any partial adoption as 'localization'. Localization is active reconstruction by local actors, not just incomplete compliance.
Ignoring the local norms and prior beliefs the external norm is grafted onto.
Assuming localization is always positive for the norm's original purpose.
